_about: Plain-language notes on the NASA PSI combustion investigations, used by the NASA research page of the console. Every summary, 'varied', 'why' and score in this file was written by an AI model (Claude) on Nov 14, 2026 from the Objectives, Approach and Keywords text of each investigation in data/raw/psi_search/combustion_investigations.json, plus the Space Apps challenge brief where the 'why' says so. They are a reading of NASA's text, not NASA's words. Scores: 3 = this need is a stated objective of the investigation; 2 = it measures limits or data that feed this need directly; 1 = related basic science, indirect link; 0 = not about this need.

excluded.PSI-108: Returned by the PSI search for 'combustion' but listed under Fluid Physics.
excluded.PSI-181: Returned by the PSI search for 'combustion' but listed under Materials Science.

PSI-26.name: BASS
PSI-26.summary: Burned fabric, plastic, spheres and cylinders in a small wind tunnel on the ISS to see how real materials spread flame and go out when the air barely moves.
PSI-26.varied: Material and shape, air flow up to 40 cm/s with or against the flame, an inert extinguishing gas.
PSI-26.why: Checks whether NASA's ground flammability test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) matches what materials do in orbit, and how well an inert-gas extinguisher like the one on the ISS puts the flames out.

PSI-25.name: BASS-II
PSI-25.summary: Follow-on to BASS with thicker, more realistic samples (rods, slabs, films, fabric sheets) in the same ISS wind tunnel, measuring ignition, flame growth, spread and extinction limits.
PSI-25.varied: Air flow speed and direction, oxygen below 21 % (nitrogen added), sample shape.
PSI-25.why: Gives the extinction limits of solid materials against oxygen and air flow, which is what material selection depends on, and feeds the models used to design detection and suppression systems.

PSI-98.name: Saffire-I
PSI-98.summary: Lit a cotton-fiberglass sheet about 0.94 m long and 0.4 m wide inside an uncrewed Cygnus cargo ship after it left the ISS, to see how fast a large fire grows in low gravity.
PSI-98.varied: One large sample at an air flow of 20 cm/s.
PSI-98.why: A large-scale fire test in space: fire growth rate and low-gravity flammability limits, compared with NASA's normal-gravity material screening test.

PSI-99.name: Saffire-II
PSI-99.summary: Second Cygnus fire test, with nine smaller samples of different materials (cotton-fiberglass, silicone, acrylic, acrylic with Nomex), each 5 cm by 29 cm.
PSI-99.varied: Material, air flow of 20 or 30 cm/s, with or against the flame.
PSI-99.why: Compares the low-gravity flammability limits of several spacecraft materials with NASA's normal-gravity screening test.

PSI-100.name: Saffire-III
PSI-100.summary: Repeat of the large Saffire-I fabric burn in a Cygnus cargo ship at a faster air flow, 30 cm/s instead of 20.
PSI-100.varied: Air flow speed and direction on the large cotton-fiberglass sample.
PSI-100.why: Shows how air flow changes the growth of a large fire in low gravity.

PSI-102.name: SAME
PSI-102.summary: Overheated spacecraft materials in the ISS glovebox and measured the smoke particles they gave off, using smoke detectors and particle samplers.
PSI-102.varied: Material, sample temperature, air flow, how long the smoke aged.
PSI-102.why: The size of smoke particles decides whether a detector sees a fire early. This is the reference data on smoke in low gravity.

PSI-101.name: SAME-R
PSI-101.summary: Reflight of SAME with fixes: a new test material (a fire-retardant foam), wider heating conditions and a new instrument. 66 test points in 2010.
PSI-101.varied: Material, heating temperature, flow or no flow while heating.
PSI-101.why: Completes the smoke particle-size data that SAME started, after contamination made the first particle samples unusable.

PSI-47.name: DAFT / DAFT-2
PSI-47.summary: Checked that a modified commercial particle counter works without gravity, by counting test dust in bags on the ISS and comparing with a second instrument.
PSI-47.varied: A dust standard measured by two instruments.
PSI-47.why: Made sure the particle counter that SAME relied on to measure smoke could be trusted in orbit.

PSI-115.name: SAME smoke modelling
PSI-115.summary: Ground study: computer simulation of how smoke particles form and grow from a heated sample, in Earth gravity and in microgravity, in a geometry like the SAME experiment.
PSI-115.varied: No new flight tests. Gravity level in the simulation.
PSI-115.why: Explains why smoke made in orbit differs from smoke made on Earth, which matters for setting detectors.

PSI-69.name: FLEX
PSI-69.summary: Burned single droplets of liquid fuel on the ISS to map the conditions where a flame can survive, and to measure how well gases such as carbon dioxide and helium put it out.
PSI-69.varied: Fuel, oxygen, pressure, suppressant gas, droplet size.
PSI-69.why: The suppression investigation: it measures how effective gaseous suppressants are and the lowest oxygen level that still supports a flame. The Flame console page is built on its test table.

PSI-68.name: FLEX-2
PSI-68.summary: Extended FLEX to fuels and conditions closer to real engines, including two-component droplets and neighbouring droplets.
PSI-68.varied: Fuel mixture, pressure 0.5 to 3 atm, oxygen 10 to 40 %, droplet arrangement.
PSI-68.why: Adds extinction boundaries and flammability limits for more fuels and for droplets burning side by side, over a wide range of pressure and oxygen.

PSI-39.name: CFI
PSI-39.summary: Studied cool flames on droplets of n-dodecane and related fuels: low-temperature burning that can carry on without a visible hot flame.
PSI-39.varied: Fuel, pressure 0.25 to 5 atm, helium dilution, droplet size.
PSI-39.why: A fire that looks out may still be reacting. Shows how pressure and helium change that hidden burning.

PSI-20.name: ACME BRE
PSI-20.summary: Used a gas burner that imitates a burning solid or liquid surface to map when a material can keep burning in still air in microgravity.
PSI-20.varied: Burner size, fuel gas, oxygen and pressure, including cabin atmospheres NASA considers for crewed missions (14.7 psia with 21 % oxygen, 10.2 psia with 26.5 %, 8.2 psia with 34 %).
PSI-20.why: Builds a flammability map for materials in the low-pressure, oxygen-rich cabin air planned for exploration missions.

PSI-10.name: ACME Flame Design
PSI-10.summary: Spherical gas flames of ethylene and methane, used to find when soot starts to form and how dilution and pressure change the flame.
PSI-10.varied: Flow rate, dilution with nitrogen or carbon dioxide, pressure.
PSI-10.why: Soot limits and the effect of inert gases help predict which flames are weak enough to go out. The link to fire safety is indirect.

PSI-21.name: ACME CLD Flame
PSI-21.summary: Gas jet flames of methane and ethylene in a slow co-flow of air, from very dilute to heavily sooting, measured to test computer models.
PSI-21.why: Better soot and extinction models carry over to fire models. The link to fire safety is indirect.

PSI-22.name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
PSI-22.summary: Applied electric fields to small gas flames to see how the field acts on the flame's ions and changes its shape, soot and stability.
PSI-22.varied: Field voltage, with or without a co-flow of air.
PSI-22.why: The challenge brief notes that the field's pull on flame ions mimicked partial gravity, a stand-in until Moon-gravity data exists.

PSI-23.name: ACME s-Flame
PSI-23.summary: Spherical flames around a porous burner fed with hydrogen, methane or ethylene mixtures, measured in detail for comparison with computer simulations.
PSI-23.varied: Fuel and diluent mixture, flow rate.
PSI-23.why: Basic data for the chemistry and transport models that fire simulations rely on.

PSI-159.name: ACME CFI-G
PSI-159.summary: Looked for the conditions where cool flames appear in gas fuels (propane, n-butane, n-pentane) on a spherical burner, supported by simulations.
PSI-159.varied: Fuel, dilution, flow rate, normal and inverse flames.
PSI-159.why: The challenge brief says these were the microgravity tests with the highest oxygen levels, up to 85 % in the burner flow.

PSI-106.name: SLICE
PSI-106.summary: Small gas jet flames in a fan-driven flow duct on the ISS, used to learn what holds a flame to its burner and when it lifts off.
PSI-106.varied: Fuel (methane, ethylene, nitrogen-diluted mixes), burner tube, air flow.
PSI-106.why: Flame stability and heat loss in microgravity compared with normal gravity. Background for fire models.

PSI-107.name: SPICE
PSI-107.summary: Gas jet flames in a co-flow of air, used to find the smoke point: the flame length at which a flame starts to release soot.
PSI-107.varied: Fuel (methane, ethylene, propane, propylene and mixtures), burner diameter, co-flow speed.
PSI-107.why: Soot release is where smoke comes from, so smoke points help predict how much smoke a fire makes.

PSI-60.name: SPICE data analysis
PSI-60.summary: Ground study that reprocessed more than 1600 SPICE flame photos to extract soot temperature and soot amount, and compared them with soot models.
PSI-60.varied: No new flight tests. Analysis of SPICE images from PSI.
PSI-60.why: Sharpens soot predictions, which feed smoke estimates.

PSI-62.name: BASS flame-spread modelling
PSI-62.summary: Ground study that developed a new way to simulate flame spreading along a solid in microgravity and checked it against the BASS experiments.
PSI-62.varied: No new flight tests. Computer model compared with BASS data.
PSI-62.why: A validated flame-spread model lets engineers predict how a material fire grows without flying every test.

PSI-117.name: Cool-flame CFD from FLEX
PSI-117.summary: Ground study that used FLEX flight data to build a 3-D simulation of droplet cool flames and to explain why repeated runs behaved differently.
PSI-117.varied: No new flight tests. Simulated heating and droplet drift.
PSI-117.why: Shows when a cool flame keeps going, turns back into a hot flame, or dies. Useful for judging whether a fire is truly out.

PSI-142.name: Cool-flame limits
PSI-142.summary: Ground study that used FLEX data, new lab experiments and simulations to chart the flammability limits of cool flames.
PSI-142.varied: Oxygen level and fuel, in lab counterflow flames and simulations.
PSI-142.why: Connects the extinction limit of the hot flame with the limit of the cool flame that can follow it.
